STIFF PERSON SYNDROM, A RARE NEUROLOGICAL
DISEASE IN LONG-TERM CARE RESIDENT.
T
. Bhatt,A .Medina-Walpole, F. J. Marshall.Geriatric Medicine,
University of Rochester, Rochester, NY.
Supported By: University of Rochester, NY
Introduction: While geriatricians provide specialized care for
aged residents in long-term care facilities, they often also care for
younger residents with chronic neurological disorders. We present a
case of a woman with Stiff Person Syndrome, a rare neuromuscular
condition that results in severe disability requiring chronic care.
Case: A 50 year old African American woman reported pain and
weakness in her lower back and legs beginning two years previously.
She required a cane within the first 6 months, and walker within the first
year. She noted involuntary flexion of her knees and progressive inabil-
ity to move her legs due to severe pain and spasms. She had no concur-
rent history of fever, mental status changes, bladder/bowel inconti-
nence, headache or joint pain. A series of diagnostic tests including
ANA, RF, thyroid and paraneoplastic panels, serial CK, CSF studies and
glutamic acid decarboxylase(GAD)antibody were all unrevealing, as
was whole body imaging.An EMG showed changes consistent with Stiff
Person Syndrome. Trials of solumedrol, immunoglobulin and plasma
exchange were given without benefit. Currently she is a resident of our
long-term care facility, requiring opioids, benzodiazepines and muscle
relaxants. She is completely dependent for her activities of daily living.
Discussion:
